lede: A jumper is in a sale at 30% off and costs £28. What was it before? You cannot take 30% off £28, because the 30% was taken off the larger, original price. Every percentage change is a multiplication, and going backwards means dividing by the same multiplier.
can: Write the multiplier for any increase or decrease.
Decide whether the number you are given comes before or after the change.
Divide by the multiplier to get back to the original.

text: Reverse percentages: finding the original quantity

md: Ten words, and the marks all turn on one of them: **result**. The number you are handed is the result, not the start. A sale price, a price including VAT, a population after growth, a value after depreciation — every one of those is the *after* value. A percentage change is a multiplication, and multiplication has exactly one inverse: division.

text: Multipliers: the whole topic in one line

md:
A percentage change is a multiplication. An increase of $r\%$ multiplies by $1 + \frac{r}{100}$; a decrease multiplies by $1 - \frac{r}{100}$.

| Change | Multiplier |
| --- | --- |
| increase 8% | 1.08 |
| increase 2.5% | 1.025 |
| decrease 15% | 0.85 |
| decrease 6.2% | 0.938 |
| VAT at 20% added | 1.2 |
| 0.5% interest | 1.005 |

Multiplication has one inverse, and it is division. That is the whole method: **forwards multiply, backwards divide**.

prompt: Write the multiplier for a decrease of 15%.

md:
A gym fee rose by 24% and is now £930. The £930 is *after* the rise, so it is 124% of the old fee. CCEA schemes print three lines and give a mark for each:
$124\% = £930$
$1\% = £930 \div 124 = £7.50$
$100\% = £7.50 \times 100 = £750$
On a calculator paper the single line $£930 \div 1.24 = £750$ earns the same three marks. Check by going forwards: $£750 \times 1.24 = £930$.

prompt: A gym fee rose by 24% and is now £930. What percentage of the old fee is £930?
explain: The rise was added on to 100%, so £930 is 124% of the old fee. Writing that line first is what turns the question into a single division.

md: **Why subtracting fails.** The 24% was worked out on the old fee of £750, so it was £180. Taking 24% of the *new* £930 gives £223.20, and £930 − £223.20 = £706.80, which is not the old fee. The bigger the percentage, the bigger the error.

text: Finding the after value inside the words

md:
The examiners' word for this is recognition. These all mean *the change has already happened*:
**sale price** or **reduced to** — below 100%; **including VAT at 20%** — 120%; **the population is now** — above 100% after growth; **depreciated**, **loss**, **discount** — below 100%; **profit of 12%** — 112% of what was paid.
Depreciation catches people every November: it means fallen in value, so a fall of 6.2% leaves 93.8%.

title: November 2025 M3 Q30 and M4 Q15
md: Candidates who wrote 93.8% = the given value usually finished. Others set that line up and then reverted to adding or subtracting 6.2%, and some started from 106.2% because 'depreciated' had not been read as a decrease.

text: When the amount you are given is a difference

md: A large coffee costs 30% more than a small one, and the **difference** is £0.66. The 66p is not 130% and it is not 100%: it is the 30%. So $30\% = £0.66$, which gives $10\% = £0.22$ and $100\% = £2.20$ for the small one — and if the question wants the large one, that is $£2.20 + £0.66 = £2.86$, which agrees with $£2.20 \times 1.3$.

explain: 35% = £9.45, so 1% = £0.27 and 100% = £27. The large tub would be £36.45.

md:
A flat sold in 2025 for £184 320, a loss of 4%; the seller had bought it from an owner who made 20% profit. Undo the most recent change first.
$96\% = £184\,320$, so she paid $£184\,320 \div 0.96 = £192\,000$.
$120\% = £192\,000$, so he paid $£192\,000 \div 1.2 = £160\,000$.
Forwards, $£160\,000 \times 1.2 \times 0.96 = £184\,320$, so both directions were read correctly.

text: A change as a percentage of the original

md:
The same relationship, read the other way. **Percentage change $= \frac{\text{change}}{\text{original}} \times 100$.** A jacket that cost £96 and now costs £120 has risen by £24, and $\frac{24}{96} \times 100 = 25\%$.
Two divisions look tempting and are not the answer: $\frac{120}{96} \times 100 = 125\%$ is the multiplier as a percentage, and $\frac{24}{120} \times 100 = 20\%$ measures the rise against the new price.

prompt: Membership rose by 84 to 684. The percentage increase is

md:
An account paying 3% in the first year and 1.5% in the second is $\times 1.03$ then $\times 1.015$, each acting on the balance at the time. £2400 becomes £2472, then £2509.08.
Adding the rates gives 4.5% and the wrong answer, because $1.03 \times 1.015 = 1.04545$. Backwards, divide by each in turn: £5227.25 ÷ 1.015 = £5150, then ÷ 1.03 = £5000. Money always carries two decimal places.

title: Why two changes need two divisions
md: Each percentage acts on the balance at the time, so the changes multiply rather than add: $1.03 \times 1.015 = 1.04545$, which is not $1.045$. Undoing them one at a time, most recent first, is the only way back.

Write the multiplier for any increase or decrease.
Say whether the number given is before or after the change.
Divide by the multiplier to get back to the original.
Undo two changes one at a time, most recent first.

This is a fixture on both calculator papers: one straight reversal of three marks, and often a four-mark version with a step after it. The first mark is the line that names the percentage — 124% = the value. The last is the quantity actually asked for, which may not be the original. Stuck: write that first line and divide; the unitary route scores the same.

title: Not on this spec
md: The compound-interest formula with an index, $P(1 + r)^n$, and questions asking for the number of years belong to M8 growth and decay (M8-NA-04). The Teacher Guidance on M2-NA-08 caps compound interest at three iterations, so no reversal here has more than three multipliers to undo. Percentage error and exponential growth to base $e$ are not CCEA content, and reverse percentages are never combined with upper and lower bounds.
